title: Spend the view’s one red on the point the title names.
rule: Rule 05.3 gives each view one working red and says which job claims it first. In a chart, the red goes to the one point, bar or line the title names, inside the 1 px Charcoal keyline of Rule 05.5, and that mark carries its own label. Every other mark takes the light fill on Newsprint and the context ink on Charcoal (Rule 05.7).

The named mark gives up the red and takes Charcoal at the subject weight, with its label, in two cases: when an error or a step the reader can take already holds the view’s red, and when a reader would tie the mark to a party. A state, a Congress or chamber whose majority readers know, an election result, a campaign’s money and a policy readers link to one party all carry that tie, and red on them reads as a party’s color (Rules 01.1, 01.2 and 14.7). Red never codes a series, a group or a step on a scale.

text: One red mark tells a reader where to look first, and the title tells them why. A second red mark splits their attention, and red that codes a group reads as a warning about that group.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the chart system our founder and editor approved in November 2026

builders: Name the one point in the spec’s labels.point, which draws it in red with its keyline, or in labels.named where a party tie gives it the subject ink; the kit counts working reds and fails a view with two.

correct.caption: The title names the Ninth Circuit, and its bar alone takes the view’s red, inside its keyline, with every other court in gray.
correct.alt: Bars of active judges on the 13 federal courts of appeals, the Ninth Circuit’s 29 in red and the rest in gray, from 17 on the Fifth Circuit down to 6 on the First Circuit.
correct.notes: Drawn here from the directory's rows, counted by script, until the kit takes a red point by name (request ED-E1).

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.6. Red falls on three courts while the title names one, so a reader cannot tell which bar the title means.
failure.alt: Failure case: do not publish. The same bars with three courts in red, the Ninth, Fifth and Sixth Circuits, under a title that names one.
